title: Math Foundations
description: Linear algebra, calculus, probability, and information theory for IOAI

questions.text: A matrix $A$ has shape (4, 3) and matrix $B$ has shape (3, 5). What is the shape of $A \times B$?
questions.explanation: Matrix multiplication (m×n) × (n×p) = (m×p). Here (4×3) × (3×5) = (4×5). The inner dimensions (3) must match and disappear from the result.

questions.text: In the equation $y = Wx + b$ for a neural network layer, what is the dimension of $W$ if the input $x$ has 512 features and the output has 256 features?
questions.explanation: The weight matrix W transforms 512 inputs to 256 outputs. Since y = Wx + b where x is (512,) and y is (256,), W must be (256, 512) to make the shapes work: (256, 512) @ (512,) = (256,).

questions.text: What does a positive dot product between two vectors tell you?
options: One vector is longer than the other
questions.explanation: The dot product a·b = |a||b|cos(θ). When the angle θ < 90°, cos(θ) > 0, so the dot product is positive. This means the vectors point roughly in the same direction — which is exactly what cosine similarity measures.

The sigmoid derivative is σ(x)(1 - σ(x)). This is why sigmoid vanishes: its maximum derivative is 0.25 (at x=0), and it falls toward 0 for large |x|. This causes the vanishing gradient problem in deep networks.

questions.text: What does the gradient of a function point toward?
options: The average of all partial derivatives
questions.explanation: The gradient ∇f points in the direction of steepest INCREASE. That's why gradient DESCENT moves in the NEGATIVE gradient direction — we go downhill by going opposite to the gradient.

questions.text: A fair coin is flipped 3 times. What is the probability of getting exactly 2 heads?
questions.explanation: C(3,2) × (0.5)² × (0.5)¹ = 3 × 0.25 × 0.5 = 3/8. The three arrangements are HHT, HTH, THH — each with probability 1/8, totaling 3/8.

questions.text: Bayes' theorem: P(A|B) = P(B|A) × P(A) / P(B). In ML terms, P(class|data) involves multiplying the __ by the __.
questions.explanation: P(class|data) ∝ P(data|class) × P(class). P(data|class) is the likelihood (how probable the data is given the class), and P(class) is the prior (baseline class probability). The posterior P(class|data) = likelihood × prior / evidence.

questions.text: A disease affects 1% of the population. A test is 95% accurate (95% true positive rate, 5% false positive rate). What is the probability you actually have the disease if you test positive?
questions.explanation: P(pos) = 0.95×0.01 + 0.05×0.99 = 0.0095 + 0.0495 = 0.059. P(disease|pos) = (0.95×0.01)/0.059 ≈ 16%. The low base rate (1%) means most positives are false alarms even with a 95% accurate test.

questions.text: Which distribution would you use to model the number of heads in 100 coin flips?
questions.explanation: Binomial counts successes in n independent Bernoulli trials. Each flip is Bernoulli; the total count across 100 flips is Binomial(n=100, p=0.5). By the CLT, it's approximately Gaussian for large n, but exactly Binomial.

questions.text: The entropy H(p) is HIGHEST when:
options: The distribution is uniform (all outcomes equally likely)
questions.explanation: Entropy measures uncertainty. Maximum uncertainty occurs when all outcomes are equally likely — a uniform distribution. When one outcome is certain (p=1), entropy = -1×log(1) = 0. Entropy increases with number of outcomes AND with uniformity.

questions.text: Binary cross-entropy loss for a single prediction is -log(p_correct). If your model assigns probability 0.01 to the correct class, the loss is approximately:
questions.explanation: -log(0.01) = log(100) ≈ 4.6. This is a very high loss because the model is confidently wrong — it gave only 1% probability to the correct answer. Compare: -log(0.99) ≈ 0.01, which is tiny because the model was nearly certain and correct.

options: p and q are identical distributions
p has higher entropy than q
both p and q are Gaussian
questions.explanation: D_KL(p||q) = H(p,q) - H(p) ≥ 0, with equality only when p = q. KL divergence measures the extra cost of using q when the true distribution is p. If q matches p exactly, there's no extra cost, so KL = 0.

questions.text: The chain rule says d/dx f(g(x)) = ?
questions.explanation: The chain rule: to differentiate a composition, differentiate the outer function at the inner function's value, then multiply by the inner function's derivative. This is exactly how backpropagation works — it chains partial derivatives from output to input.

questions.text: StandardScaler transforms features so that each feature has mean=0 and std=1. When should you fit the scaler?
options: Only on training data, then transform both train and test
Separately on both training and test data
On all data combined (train + test) for consistency
Only on test data to avoid data leakage
questions.explanation: Always fit only on training data. If you fit on test data (or all data), test statistics 'leak' into your normalization — the model has seen information about the test set. Use scaler.fit_transform(X_train) then scaler.transform(X_test).

questions.text: Cosine similarity between two vectors is defined as:
questions.explanation: Cosine similarity normalizes the dot product by both magnitudes, giving a value in [-1, 1]. It measures the angle between vectors regardless of their length — making it ideal for comparing embeddings where magnitude can vary.

questions.text: True or False: Two random variables with correlation r = 0 must be independent.
options: False — correlation only measures linear relationships
True — if r = 0, they are orthogonal and independent
False — only if both are Gaussian
questions.explanation: Correlation measures ONLY linear relationships. Variables can have r = 0 (no linear relationship) while having a strong non-linear relationship. Example: y = x² for symmetric x has r = 0 but is perfectly predictable from x.

questions.text: The Central Limit Theorem says that the mean of a large number of independent random samples, regardless of their distribution, will be approximately:
questions.explanation: The CLT: for large n, the sample mean is approximately Normal(μ, σ²/n) regardless of the original distribution. This explains why Gaussian distributions appear so often in nature and in ML — many processes are sums of many small independent contributions.

questions.text: L2 normalization of a vector divides it by its norm. After L2 normalization, what is the magnitude of the vector?
questions.explanation: L2 normalization: x_norm = x / ||x||. The magnitude of the result is ||x|| / ||x|| = 1. L2-normalized vectors lie on the unit sphere. CLIP uses L2-normalized embeddings so that cosine similarity = dot product (no need to divide by magnitudes).
